articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Sorting a Million Documents Into Piles by Meaning
articles.subtitle: BERTopic finds the themes in a pile of text by clustering sentence embeddings, then naming each cluster with its most telling words
articles.paper_title: BERTopic: Neural topic modeling with a class-based TF-IDF procedure

glossary.definition: A method that discovers the main themes in a collection of documents and describes each theme with a list of words.
A vector representing the meaning of a whole sentence or document, so similar texts get nearby vectors.
Squeezing high-dimensional vectors into a few dimensions while keeping nearby points nearby, which makes clustering easier.
Grouping points that sit in dense regions, and labelling scattered points as outliers instead of forcing them into a group.
A word score that is high when a word is frequent in one document but rare across the collection.
BERTopic's variant of TF-IDF that treats all documents in one cluster as a single long document, to find the words that characterise that cluster.

quiz.q: What are the four main steps of BERTopic, in order?
options: Embed documents, reduce dimensions, cluster, describe clusters with c-TF-IDF
quiz.explain: Documents are embedded by meaning, squeezed into fewer dimensions, clustered by density, and each cluster is then described by its most distinctive words.

quiz.q: Why does c-TF-IDF treat a whole cluster as one document?
options: So word scores reflect what is typical of the cluster compared with other clusters, giving topic keywords
Because clusters contain only one document
quiz.explain: Joining a cluster's documents lets frequency within the cluster, compared with frequency across all clusters, pick out the words that define it.

quiz.q: What is a known limitation of BERTopic's basic approach?
options: It assigns each document to a single topic, although real documents often mix several
quiz.explain: Clustering puts each document in one group, so a document about both sport and politics must pick one. The paper notes this assumption.

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Teaching an Autoencoder to Dream
articles.subtitle: Variational autoencoders: fuzzy codes, a smooth map of possibilities, and one clever trick that made it trainable
articles.paper_title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes

glossary.definition: A model that learns the patterns of a dataset well enough to create new examples that look like they came from it.
The hidden space of codes a model uses to describe its data. Points in it correspond to possible outputs.
The distribution the model assumes codes come from before seeing any data, here a simple bell curve centred on zero.
Writing a random sample as a fixed formula plus independent noise, so gradients can flow through the sampling step.
A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another. Zero means they are identical.
The objective a VAE maximizes: how well it reconstructs the data, minus a penalty for codes that stray from the prior. Often called the ELBO.

quiz.q: How does a VAE's encoder differ from a plain autoencoder's?
options: It outputs a single exact code
It outputs a small cloud of possible codes, described by a mean and a spread
It outputs the label of the image
quiz.explain: Each input maps to a distribution over codes. Sampling from it forces nearby codes to decode into similar outputs.

quiz.q: Why is the reparameterization trick needed?
options: Because you cannot backpropagate through a random sampling step directly; rewriting it as mean plus spread times noise makes it differentiable
quiz.explain: With z = mu + sigma times epsilon, the randomness lives in epsilon, and gradients can flow to mu and sigma.

quiz.q: What does the KL term in the VAE objective encourage?
options: Codes that stay close to a simple standard bell curve, keeping the latent space smooth and free of holes
quiz.explain: By pulling every input's code cloud toward the same simple prior, the KL term makes the space continuous, so random points decode to sensible outputs.

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Counterfeiter and the Detective
articles.subtitle: Generative adversarial nets: two networks locked in a game, and an idea sketched in a Montreal bar that learned to fake reality
articles.paper_title: Generative Adversarial Nets

glossary.definition: The network in a GAN that turns random noise into fake samples, trying to make them indistinguishable from real data.
The network in a GAN that looks at a sample and outputs the probability that it is real rather than generated.
Training two models against each other, so that each one's improvement forces the other to improve.
A two-player game where one player tries to maximize a score that the other tries to minimize.
A GAN failure where the generator produces only a few kinds of outputs, ignoring much of the variety in the real data.
A list of random numbers fed into the generator. Different noise vectors produce different generated samples.

quiz.q: What does the discriminator in a GAN do?
options: Estimates whether a sample is real data or a fake from the generator
quiz.explain: It is the detective: it outputs the probability that its input came from the real dataset.

quiz.q: According to the paper's theory, what happens at the ideal end of training?
options: The discriminator wins and always detects fakes
The generator's samples match the real data distribution, and the discriminator can only guess, outputting one half everywhere
The generator copies the training set exactly
quiz.explain: At the theoretical optimum, fakes and real data are indistinguishable, so the best possible detective is a coin flip.

quiz.q: What is mode collapse?
options: The generator producing only a narrow set of outputs instead of the full variety of the data
quiz.explain: A generator can fool the discriminator by perfecting a few outputs, so it stops exploring the full range of real data.

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Creating Images by Removing Noise
articles.subtitle: Denoising diffusion: destroy a picture with static, step by step, then train a network to run the film backwards
articles.paper_title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

glossary.definition: A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process, turning pure random noise into a realistic sample step by step.
The fixed procedure that adds a little Gaussian noise to an image at each of many steps until only noise remains.
The learned procedure that removes noise step by step, starting from pure noise and ending with a clean image.
Random values drawn from a bell curve, like the static on an old television screen.
The plan for how much noise to add at each step of the forward process.
Fréchet Inception Distance: a score comparing the statistics of generated images with real ones. Lower is better.

quiz.q: What does the network in a diffusion model learn to predict during training?
options: The noise that was added to a noisy image
Whether an image is real or fake
The next pixel from left to right
quiz.explain: Given a noisy image and the step number, the network predicts the noise, which can then be subtracted out.

quiz.q: How do you generate a brand-new image with a trained diffusion model?
options: Start from a random training image
Start from pure random noise and repeatedly apply the learned denoising step
Ask a discriminator to approve it
quiz.explain: Sampling runs the reverse process: begin with static and remove a little predicted noise at each of many steps.

quiz.q: What was the main practical drawback of the original DDPM?
options: Slow sampling, since generating one image took about a thousand network evaluations
quiz.explain: Quality was excellent, but each sample required running the network once per step, around 1,000 times.

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Diffusion in a Smaller World
articles.subtitle: Latent diffusion: compress the image first, dream in the compressed space, and suddenly anyone can generate art on a gaming PC
articles.paper_title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

glossary.definition: A compressed representation of images where each image becomes a much smaller grid of numbers that still captures its content.
Shrinking an image while keeping everything that matters to a human viewer, discarding fine pixel-level detail that the eye barely notices.
A pair of networks: an encoder that compresses an image into a small code, and a decoder that rebuilds the image from it.
Attention where one set of things, like image regions, looks up information in another, like the words of a text prompt.
Giving a generative model extra information, such as a caption or a class label, to steer what it creates.
A sampling trick that compares the model's predictions with and without the prompt and pushes further in the prompt's direction, making images follow text more closely.

quiz.q: What is the key efficiency idea of latent diffusion?
options: Run the diffusion process on a small compressed representation instead of full-resolution pixels
Generate only black and white images
quiz.explain: An autoencoder first compresses images, so the expensive diffusion steps work on a grid many times smaller.

quiz.q: How does a text prompt steer the image in a latent diffusion model?
options: The text is pasted onto the image
Cross-attention layers inside the denoising U-Net let image regions look up information from the encoded prompt
The prompt changes the random seed only
quiz.explain: At each denoising step, the network attends to the text encoding, so the words shape what emerges from the noise.

quiz.q: Why does the autoencoder only need to be trained once?
options: Because the same compressed space can be reused for many diffusion models and tasks
quiz.explain: The compression stage is separate and general, so different diffusion models for different tasks can all share it.

glossary.definition: A generator decomposed into cascaded networks where lower-resolution representations provide global context to subsequent networks that synthesize higher-resolution local detail.
Multiple discriminator networks of identical architecture applied to downsampled versions of an image pyramid to simultaneously capture global consistency and fine texture details.
A training loss computed by taking the L1 distance between intermediate layer activations of the discriminator for real versus generated images.
A binary edge map identifying the pixel borders between distinct individual object instances of the same semantic class.

quiz.q: Why does the framework use three discriminators operating at different scales rather than one large discriminator?
options: A single discriminator would require an impractically deep network or huge receptive field, increasing memory and risking overfitting.
A single discriminator cannot compute gradient backpropagation on GPUs.
Using multiple discriminators is required to calculate the cross-entropy loss between multiple labels.
Three discriminators are necessary to process red, green, and blue color channels independently.
quiz.explain: A discriminator needs a vast receptive field to evaluate 2048x1024 images globally. Increasing kernel size or depth blows up parameter count and GPU memory, whereas an image pyramid lets small discriminators inspect both global context and fine local details.

quiz.q: How does pix2pixHD prevent adjacent objects of the same class (like parked cars) from merging into a single blob?
options: By enforcing a contrastive loss between different color clusters.
By computing an instance boundary map and appending it to the semantic segmentation channels.
By increasing the learning rate of the local enhancer network.
By downsampling the semantic mask by 4x before feeding it to the generator.
quiz.explain: Because pure semantic label maps assign the same class ID to neighboring cars, the authors extract 1-pixel instance boundary maps from instance IDs and concatenate them with the label input.

quiz.q: In the discriminator feature matching loss, what role does the discriminator play regarding the feature matching term?
options: The discriminator maximizes the feature matching loss to increase divergence.
The discriminator updates its weights to make real and fake features as far apart as possible.
The discriminator acts solely as a static feature extractor; only the generator minimizes this loss.
The discriminator discards all convolutional layers and uses fully connected projections.
quiz.explain: The paper explicitly notes that for the feature matching loss LFM, the discriminator Dk only serves as a feature extractor and does not maximize LFM; only the generator G minimizes it to match natural statistics.

glossary.definition: A generative model trained to remove noise step by step, so it can turn pure noise into a realistic image.
The fixed recipe that gradually adds noise to a training image until it becomes pure noise.
A sequence of steps where each step depends only on the one just before it.
A way of generating where the same starting noise always produces exactly the same image, because no fresh randomness is added along the way.
The starting noise image from which a sample is generated. With a deterministic sampler it acts like a code for the final image.
The trained network that looks at a noisy image and estimates the noise that was added to it.

quiz.q: Why could DDIM reuse models already trained as DDPMs?
options: It uses a different loss that happens to match
Its new family of forward processes has the same single-step noise levels, so the DDPM training objective still applies
It only works on new models
quiz.explain: The training loss only depends on how noisy an image is at each step, which DDIM keeps the same. Only the sampling procedure changes.

quiz.q: What happens when DDIM's randomness parameter is set to zero?
options: The same starting noise always gives the same image
quiz.explain: With no fresh noise added during sampling, the path from noise to image is fixed, so the starting noise acts like a code for the image.

quiz.q: What was DDIM's main practical benefit?
options: Good samples in far fewer steps, for example 50 instead of 1,000
Removing the need for a neural network
quiz.explain: By skipping steps along a deterministic path, DDIM produced good images 10 to 50 times faster than the original sampler.

glossary.definition: A learned list of vectors, each standing for a visual pattern. Every patch of an image is replaced by the index of its closest codebook vector.
Replacing a continuous vector with the nearest entry in a fixed codebook, turning it into a whole-number index.
Generating a sequence one element at a time, each predicted from all the elements before it.
A loss that compares images by features from a pre-trained vision network, so it rewards looking similar rather than matching pixel by pixel.
A GAN discriminator that judges many small regions of an image as real or fake, pushing the decoder to produce sharp local detail.
One element of a sequence a transformer reads. Here, one codebook index standing for a patch of the image.

quiz.q: Why not run a transformer directly on pixels of a 256 by 256 image?
options: That is 65,536 pixels per colour channel, and attention cost grows with the square of sequence length
quiz.explain: Attention compares every position with every other. A sequence of tens of thousands of pixels is far too long, which is why VQGAN compresses the image to a 16 by 16 grid of tokens.

quiz.q: What do the adversarial and perceptual losses add to the VQ autoencoder?
options: Sharp, realistic detail even when the image is compressed into very few tokens
quiz.explain: Plain pixel losses give blurry reconstructions at high compression. Perceptual and patch-based adversarial losses reward realistic textures, so a short code can still decode into a crisp image.

quiz.q: How does the model generate images larger than its training size?
options: The transformer predicts tokens with a sliding attention window over the token grid
It trains a new model for each size
quiz.explain: Each new token only attends to a local window of previous tokens, so generation can continue across a grid much larger than seen in training.

glossary.definition: The plan for how much noise is added at each step of the forward process, from almost none to pure noise.
How spread out a random value is. Here, how much fresh randomness the model adds at each step of generation.
A score for how probable the model thinks real data is. Higher means the model covers the data distribution better.
A quantity that is always below the true log-likelihood, so maximising it pushes the likelihood up. Often abbreviated VLB.
Fréchet Inception Distance, a common score for generated images that compares their statistics to real images. Lower is better.
For generative models, how much of the variety in the real data the generated samples cover.

quiz.q: What did the paper let the network learn that DDPM had fixed by hand?
options: The variance of each reverse step, interpolated between two sensible bounds
quiz.explain: DDPM fixed the reverse-step variance to a constant. Learning it, as a blend between two known bounds, improved likelihood and allowed sampling with fewer steps.

quiz.q: Why replace the linear noise schedule with a cosine one?
options: The linear schedule destroyed information too quickly, so many late steps were nearly pure noise and wasted
It was required for learned variances
quiz.explain: With the linear schedule, images, especially small ones, became almost pure noise well before the final steps. The cosine schedule adds noise more evenly.

quiz.q: Compared with BigGAN at similar FID, what did the diffusion model show?
options: Higher recall, meaning it covered more of the data's variety
quiz.explain: GANs often miss parts of the distribution. The paper found diffusion models achieved better recall, a sign of fuller coverage.

glossary.definition: A deterministic ordinary differential equation whose trajectories share the same marginal probability densities as a stochastic diffusion process.
An objective that trains a network to estimate the score by learning to denoise samples corrupted with known Gaussian noise.
A numerical integration technique that uses a predictor Euler step followed by a trapezoidal corrector step to cut down error.
The count of forward passes through the score network needed to generate an image, measuring computational cost directly.
Scaling network inputs, targets, and skip connections so that training targets keep unit variance across all noise levels.
Temporarily adding new noise during an ODE step and removing it to correct accumulated discretization errors.

quiz.q: Why does setting the schedule to σ(t) = t and s(t) = 1 straighten the ODE solution trajectories?
options: It cancels all non-linear activation functions inside the denoiser network.
A single Euler step toward t = 0 directly points to the denoiser output, which changes slowly across noise levels.
It eliminates Gaussian noise from the initial state completely.
It guarantees that the neural network only needs to predict pure white noise.
quiz.explain: When σ(t) = t and s(t) = 1, the ODE derivative points straight at the denoised estimate D(x; t). Because that estimate changes slowly across noise levels, the trajectories become nearly linear.

quiz.q: What is the primary benefit of preconditioning the raw network with σ-dependent skip connections?
options: It keeps the network training target at unit variance instead of amplifying errors by multiplying by noise at high noise levels.
It eliminates the need to calculate backpropagation gradients for convolutional layers.
It ensures sampling can be executed in exactly one Euler step.
It replaces the need for score matching with adversarial training.
quiz.explain: Without skip-connection scaling, predicting raw noise forces the network to cancel out huge noise values at large σ, where tiny errors blow up. Preconditioning keeps targets scaled to unit variance across all noise scales.

quiz.q: What happened to stochastic sampling on CIFAR-10 once training preconditioning and loss weighting were fixed?
options: Stochastic sampling became strictly mandatory to avoid mode collapse.
Stochastic sampling was beneficial only when the step count exceeded 10,000 NFE.
Stochastic sampling became unnecessary and even detrimental compared to deterministic sampling.
Stochastic sampling had zero effect on FID regardless of noise level.
quiz.explain: Once the model was properly trained with the right preconditioning and noise distribution, deterministic sampling achieved the best FID on CIFAR-10; adding stochastic noise churn actively degraded image quality.

glossary.definition: Learning by trial and error: an agent takes actions in an environment and learns from the rewards it receives.
The learner that observes the environment and chooses actions.
A number the environment gives the agent after an action, such as points in a game. The agent tries to collect as much as possible over time.
An estimate of the total future reward you will get if you take a particular action in a particular situation and play well afterwards.
Storing past experiences in a memory and training on random samples from it, instead of only on the latest moment.
A slowly updated copy of the network used to compute training targets, which keeps learning stable.
Trying actions that are not currently believed to be best, in order to discover better strategies.

quiz.q: What did DQN receive as input when playing Atari games?
options: Raw screen pixels and the game score

quiz.q: Why does DQN use experience replay?
options: To break the strong correlation between consecutive frames and reuse each experience many times
To make the game run faster
quiz.explain: Training on random past moments, rather than a stream of nearly identical consecutive frames, makes learning far more stable and data-efficient.

quiz.q: What does a Q-value represent?
options: The expected total future reward of taking an action in a state and acting well afterwards
quiz.explain: Q-values look ahead: they include the immediate reward plus discounted future rewards.

A search method that explores possible future move sequences by simulating many games, focusing effort on the most promising lines.
Training a game-playing system by having it play against copies of itself.

Playing a game out quickly to the end from some position, using a fast simple policy, to estimate who would win.

quiz.q: What did AlphaGo's policy network do?
options: Suggest which moves are promising in a given position
Count the stones on the board

options: Go has far more possible moves per turn and longer games, and positions are very hard to evaluate
Computers cannot draw a Go board

glossary.definition: The agent's strategy: a function that, given a situation, gives the probability of taking each possible action.
A family of methods that directly adjust the policy, making actions that led to good outcomes more likely.
How much better an action turned out than what the agent expected on average in that situation. Positive means better than expected.
The new policy's probability of an action divided by the old policy's probability. A ratio of 1.2 means the action became 20% more likely.
Limiting a number to a range. PPO clips the probability ratio so a single update cannot change the policy too much.
A zone around the current policy within which updates are considered safe, because the data collected by the old policy still describes them well.

quiz.q: What problem does PPO's clipping solve?
options: Destructively large policy updates that can collapse performance
quiz.explain: If one update changes the policy too much, the agent can suddenly perform terribly. Clipping removes the incentive to move far from the old policy.

quiz.q: If an action had a positive advantage, what does the policy gradient try to do?
quiz.explain: Positive advantage means the action worked better than expected, so the policy should choose it more often.

quiz.q: Why was PPO preferred over TRPO by many practitioners?
options: It gave theoretical guarantees TRPO lacked
It achieved similar stability with a much simpler, first-order method that is easy to implement
It does not need any data
quiz.explain: TRPO enforced its trust region with complex second-order maths. PPO approximates the same behaviour with a clipped objective and ordinary gradient descent.

glossary.definition: A way for a model to decide which parts of the input matter most for each output, by giving every part a weight and mixing them together.
Attention where every word in a sentence looks at every other word in the same sentence to understand its context.
A small chunk of text, like a word or part of a word, that the model reads as one unit.
An older kind of network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward from each step to the next.
Three vectors made from each token. The query says what a token is looking for, the key says what it offers, and the value is the information it passes on.
A function that turns a list of scores into positive weights that add up to 1, so bigger scores get bigger shares.
Extra numbers added to each token's embedding so the model knows where in the sentence the token sits.
A standard score for machine translation that measures how much a system's output overlaps with human translations. Higher is better.

quiz.q: What did the Transformer remove that earlier translation models depended on?
options: Recurrence, reading words one at a time
quiz.explain: Transformers process all tokens at once with self-attention instead of stepping through the sentence word by word.

quiz.q: In self-attention, what decides how much one word listens to another?
options: How well the first word's query matches the second word's key
A fixed table written by the researchers
quiz.explain: Each word's query is compared with every key using a dot product. Higher scores become bigger attention weights after the softmax.

quiz.q: Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?
options: To make training slower but more accurate
Because attention on its own has no sense of word order
To translate between languages with different alphabets
To reduce the number of parameters
quiz.explain: Attention treats the input as a set. Without position information, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look identical.

glossary.definition: A model that predicts the next token in a piece of text, given the tokens before it.
Training a model on a huge amount of unlabeled data with a general task, like next-word prediction, before adapting it to specific tasks.
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller labeled dataset for a particular task.
Reusing what a model learned on one task to do better on another, usually with much less data.
A Transformer that keeps only the decoder half, where each token can attend to the tokens before it but not after it.
A chunk of text, often a word or a piece of a word, that the model reads as one unit.
Performing a task without any task-specific training examples.

quiz.q: What task was GPT pre-trained on?
options: Predicting the next token in a large collection of books
quiz.explain: The model learned language by predicting the next token across thousands of unpublished books, with no labels needed.

quiz.q: How did GPT handle different tasks like entailment or multiple-choice questions?
options: A completely different architecture for each task
By converting each task's inputs into a single sequence of text with special separator tokens, then adding a small output layer
By retraining from scratch for each task
quiz.explain: Task-specific input formatting let the same pre-trained Transformer handle many tasks with minimal changes.

quiz.q: Which kind of Transformer did GPT use?
options: Encoder only, reading in both directions
Decoder only, where each token sees only earlier tokens
quiz.explain: GPT kept the decoder, with masked attention, which is natural for predicting the next word.

glossary.definition: Able to use context from both the left and the right of a word at the same time.
A pre-training task where some words in a sentence are hidden and the model must predict them from the surrounding words.
BERT's second pre-training task: given two sentences, predict whether the second really follows the first in the original text.
The half of a Transformer where every token can attend to every other token, producing a contextual vector for each one.
Briefly training a pre-trained model on a specific labeled task, usually updating all of its weights.
A vector for a word that depends on the sentence it appears in, so 'bank' in 'river bank' and 'bank loan' get different vectors.

quiz.q: Why couldn't BERT simply be trained to predict the next word, like GPT?
options: With full bidirectional attention, each word could see itself and the answer, so the task would be trivial

quiz.q: In BERT's masked language model, what happens to the selected 15% of tokens?
options: All are deleted from the sentence
Most become a [MASK] token, some become a random word, and some stay unchanged
They are moved to the end of the sentence
quiz.explain: 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% stay the same, so the model cannot rely on always seeing [MASK] during pre-training.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a contextual embedding over a word2vec vector?
options: The same word gets different vectors depending on its sentence, capturing its meaning in context
quiz.explain: BERT's output for 'bank' changes with the surrounding words, which resolves ambiguity that a single fixed vector cannot.

Giving a model a handful of worked examples of a task in its prompt before asking it to do a new one.
Asking a model to do a task from an instruction alone, with no examples.
One of the learned numbers inside a model. GPT-3 has about 175 billion of them.

The model picking up a task from examples in its prompt, with no weight updates
Training a model in a classroom

glossary.definition: A simple mathematical relationship describing how a model's performance changes as you scale up its size, data or compute.
A relationship of the form y = a times x to the power b. On a log-log plot it appears as a straight line.
A chart where both axes use a logarithmic scale, so each step along an axis means multiplying by ten.
The total amount of calculation used to train a model, usually counted in floating point operations (FLOPs).
The model's average next-token prediction loss on text it was not trained on. Lower means better language modelling.
How much a model learns from each example it sees. A more sample-efficient model reaches a given loss with less data.

quiz.q: What did the paper find about how loss depends on model size?
options: Loss stops improving after 1 billion parameters
Loss falls as a smooth power law, a straight line on a log-log plot, across many orders of magnitude

Very little: within a wide range, total parameter count mattered far more than shape
The number of attention heads above all

quiz.q: What did the paper recommend for a fixed compute budget?
options: Train a small model for a very long time
Train a very large model and stop well before it fully converges
Spend most of the compute on data cleaning
Never train beyond one epoch of a small dataset
quiz.explain: Larger models are more sample-efficient, so the paper concluded it was best to scale models up and stop early. Chinchilla later revised how the budget should be split.

glossary.definition: The choice of model size and amount of training data that gives the lowest loss for a fixed training compute budget.
The total number of tokens of text a model processes during training.
Floating point operations: the basic arithmetic steps a computer performs. Total training FLOPs measure training compute.
A set of models trained with the same total compute but different sizes, used to find which size gives the lowest loss for that budget.

Using a trained model to produce outputs. Smaller models are cheaper and faster at inference.

quiz.q: What was Chinchilla's main finding about compute-optimal training?
options: Model size should grow much faster than data
Model size and training tokens should be scaled up in roughly equal proportion
Models should never be larger than 1 billion parameters
quiz.explain: If you double the compute-optimal model size, you should roughly double the number of training tokens too.

quiz.q: How did Chinchilla (70B parameters) compare with Gopher (280B parameters)?
options: It used the same compute budget, was four times smaller, saw about four times more data, and performed better
It used ten times more compute
quiz.explain: Same compute, different split: a smaller model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens beat the bigger one trained on 300 billion.

quiz.q: Why does a smaller, well-trained model matter after training too?
options: It is cheaper and faster to run for every user query
It needs more GPUs to serve
quiz.explain: Inference costs scale with model size, so a smaller model with the same quality is much cheaper to deploy.

glossary.definition: A small square piece of an image, such as 16 by 16 pixels, treated as one token by the Vision Transformer.
The vector made by flattening a patch's pixels and passing them through a learned linear layer.
Assumptions built into a model's design, like a convolutional network's assumption that nearby pixels matter most.
An extra learnable token added to the sequence whose final vector is used to classify the whole image.
A learned vector added to each patch embedding so the model knows where in the image the patch came from.
The large collection of images a model learns from first, before being fine-tuned on a specific task.

quiz.q: How does the Vision Transformer turn an image into a sequence?
options: It reads pixels one by one
It splits the image into fixed-size patches, flattens each, and projects it into a vector, like a word embedding
It converts the image to a caption first
It uses a convolutional network to describe each object
quiz.explain: A 224 by 224 image with 16 by 16 patches becomes a sequence of 196 patch tokens.

quiz.q: Why did ViT underperform ResNets when trained only on ImageNet's 1.3 million images?
options: It lacks the built-in assumptions of convolutions, so it needs more data to learn them
quiz.explain: Convolutions bake in locality and translation equivariance. ViT has to learn such patterns from data, which takes more examples.

quiz.q: What happened when ViT was pre-trained on very large datasets?
options: It still lost badly to ResNets
It matched or beat state-of-the-art convolutional networks while using less compute to pre-train
It only worked on black and white images
quiz.explain: With 14 million or 300 million images, the lack of built-in bias stopped mattering, and scale won.

glossary.definition: Training a model to pull matching pairs together and push non-matching pairs apart in an embedding space.
A single vector space where both images and texts are placed, so a picture and a sentence describing it end up close together.
Classifying images into categories the model was never explicitly trained on, by comparing images with text descriptions of each category.
Learning from the free-form text that naturally accompanies images online, instead of from a fixed list of labels.
A score from -1 to 1 measuring how closely two vectors point in the same direction.
When the data a model is used on looks different from the data it was trained on, such as sketches instead of photos.

quiz.q: What is CLIP trained to do?
options: Match each image in a batch with its correct caption, among many wrong ones
Label images with one of 1,000 ImageNet classes
quiz.explain: CLIP learns by contrast: correct image-caption pairs should score high, mismatched pairs low.

quiz.q: How does CLIP classify images zero-shot?
options: By retraining on each new dataset
By turning each class name into a sentence like 'a photo of a dog', embedding it, and picking the class whose text is closest to the image
By counting pixels of each colour
quiz.explain: The text encoder creates a classifier on the fly from class names, with no task-specific training.

quiz.q: What was one notable weakness of CLIP?
options: It could not recognise any common objects
It struggled with tasks like counting objects and with some specialised or abstract tasks, such as handwritten digits
It needed labeled ImageNet data to work
It only worked on black-and-white images
quiz.explain: The paper notes poor performance on systematic tasks like counting and on datasets unlike its web training data, such as MNIST.

glossary.definition: A learnable vector appended alongside image patch tokens and the class token, trained specifically to reproduce the predictions of a teacher model through self-attention.
A distillation variant where the student learns from the single highest-scoring class chosen by the teacher rather than a smoothed probability distribution over all classes.
A data sampling strategy that feeds multiple differently augmented views of the same original image within a single training mini-batch.
Assumptions built directly into a model's architecture, such as spatial locality in convolutions, that guide learning without requiring billions of examples.
Combining separate prediction heads at inference time, such as adding the class token logits to the distillation token logits, to make a final decision.

quiz.q: Why does using a convolutional network as a teacher yield better DeiT students than using another transformer?
options: Convnets output higher-precision floating point numbers than transformers.
The convnet transfers spatial inductive biases like locality that the transformer student lacks.
Convnets have drastically more parameters than transformers, providing richer representations.
Transformers cannot compute cross-entropy loss against other transformers.
quiz.explain: Transformers lack built-in spatial assumptions like locality and translation invariance. Distilling from a convolutional teacher injects these beneficial priors into the transformer student.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the distillation token from simply adding a second class token?
options: The distillation token bypasses all self-attention layers and connects directly to the final MLP.
The distillation token is fixed and non-trainable during backpropagation.
The distillation token is supervised by the teacher model's predictions, preventing it from collapsing into the class token.
The distillation token only attends to patch tokens, ignoring the class token.
quiz.explain: Two class tokens trained on the same true labels quickly collapse to nearly identical vectors. Supervising the distillation token with the teacher's prediction forces it to learn complementary visual cues.

quiz.q: Which data regularization method was intentionally excluded from DeiT's default training recipe?
quiz.explain: The authors found that strong augmentations like Mixup and Rand-Augment were vital, but dropout degraded accuracy and was removed.

articles.title: Shift the Window, Scale the Vision
articles.subtitle: How hierarchical shifted windows let Transformers conquer high-resolution images
articles.paper_title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
articles.venue: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision

glossary.definition: Window-based Multi-Head Self-Attention, computing self-attention strictly inside local non-overlapping spatial windows.
Shifted Window Multi-Head Self-Attention, shifting the window partition grid to connect neighboring windows across consecutive layers.
An operation that combines neighboring patch tokens to reduce spatial resolution while expanding channel dimensions.
A tensor rearrangement that wraps edge fragments around a grid so shifted windows can be computed in standard batches.
A learnable offset added to attention scores based on the spatial distance between two tokens.

quiz.q: Why is standard Vision Transformer (ViT) self-attention computationally intractable for high-resolution dense vision tasks?
options: Its computational complexity scales quadratically with the total number of image patches.
It cannot compute backward passes on modern GPUs.
It requires image inputs to be strictly black and white.
Convolutional heads must be added to every layer to avoid gradient vanishing.
quiz.explain: Standard multi-head self-attention computes relationships between every pair of patches across the whole image, creating O((hw)^2) complexity which becomes prohibitive at high resolutions.

quiz.q: What is the primary function of alternating between regular (W-MSA) and shifted (SW-MSA) window partitioning?
options: To randomly drop tokens for regularization like Dropout.
To allow information to flow across window boundaries while keeping linear computational complexity.
To increase the image resolution dynamically at each layer.
To avoid needing an MLP block in the Transformer architecture.
quiz.explain: Regular window attention confines computation within disconnected windows; shifting the window boundaries in the next layer introduces connections between previously separated windows without increasing complexity.

quiz.q: How does Swin Transformer handle the variable and smaller window sizes caused by shifting the partition grid?
options: By running sliding-window convolutions over boundary regions.
By applying a cyclic shift toward the top-left and using attention masks to prevent unrelated sub-windows from attending to each other.
By interpolating the missing patches using bi-cubic upsampling.
quiz.explain: Swin uses a cyclic shift to assemble boundary pieces into regular M x M windows, paired with a masking mechanism that restricts self-attention within contiguous sub-windows.

articles.title: Teaching One Model to See, Read, and Write

articles.paper_title: BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training for Unified Vision-Language Understanding and Generation

glossary.definition: Multimodal mixture of Encoder-Decoder, a unified architecture that operates as a unimodal text encoder, an image-grounded text encoder, or an image-grounded text decoder.
Captioning and Filtering, a bootstrapping pipeline where a fine-tuned decoder writes synthetic captions and a fine-tuned classifier discards mismatched web and synthetic texts.
Image-Text Contrastive loss, an objective that aligns visual and linguistic feature spaces by pulling matching image-text pairs together and pushing non-matching pairs apart.
Image-Text Matching loss, a binary classification objective using cross-attention to predict whether a specific image and sentence truly match.
A text decoding technique that samples tokens from the smallest subset whose cumulative probability exceeds a probability threshold p.

quiz.q: Why did BLIP share all text transformer parameters except the self-attention layers?
options: Cross-attention cannot mathematically work with causal masks.
Encoders need bidirectional self-attention to read context, while decoders need causal self-attention to generate tokens.
Sharing self-attention causes out-of-memory errors on GPU clusters.
Feed-forward networks are task-specific and cannot be shared across modes.
quiz.explain: The fundamental difference between encoding a full sentence and generating new words lies in self-attention: encoders look everywhere at once, whereas decoders must only look backward at past tokens.

quiz.q: Why did nucleus sampling generate better synthetic training data than beam search in CapFilt?
options: Nucleus sampling is deterministic and eliminated all noise.
Nucleus sampling generated more diverse, surprising descriptions that introduced richer learning signals.
Beam search produced too many grammatical syntax errors.
Nucleus sampling trained the captioner with fewer parameters.
quiz.explain: Beam search generated safe, generic, repetitive captions that added little new knowledge. Even though nucleus sampling had a slightly higher noise ratio, its variety taught the model far more.

quiz.q: What went wrong when the Captioner and Filter shared neural network weights during CapFilt?
options: The model suffered from confirmation bias, causing the filter to accept faulty captions written by its own shared weights.
The filter rejected every synthetic caption produced by the captioner.
The model failed to converge during the Image-Text Contrastive training phase.
Training time doubled due to gradient conflicts.
quiz.explain: Sharing parameters caused confirmation bias: because the filter shared the captioner's worldview, it rarely flagged the captioner's errors, allowing bad synthetic text into the final training dataset.

glossary.definition: A distributed training technique that splits model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs rather than replicating them on every device.
A technique in mixed-precision training that multiplies loss by a changing factor to keep tiny gradient values from vanishing to zero.
An open-source training codebase developed by Meta AI to train large-scale language models efficiently across GPU clusters.
A benchmark measuring stereotypical bias across social groups by comparing sentence pairs that differ only in demographic terms.
A text generation method that samples only from the smallest pool of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a cutoff threshold p.

quiz.q: Why was OPT-175B able to match GPT-3 with roughly one-seventh of the estimated carbon footprint?
options: It trained on far fewer total tokens using an early-exit architecture
It used newer A100 GPUs and high compute utilization via FSDP and Megatron tensor parallelism
It switched from dense attention to sparse Mixture-of-Experts routing
It bypassed backpropagation in the first 32 layers of the network
quiz.explain: OPT-175B ran on NVIDIA A100 GPUs using efficient distributed training, reaching 147 TFLOP/s per GPU and consuming an estimated 75 tons of CO2eq compared to 500 tons for GPT-3.

quiz.q: What early warning sign reliably warned the authors that training loss was about to explode?
options: GPU memory usage dropped suddenly to zero across all worker nodes
The dynamic loss scale collapsed toward zero while final-layer activation norms surged upward
The vocabulary size doubled automatically after encountering unnormalized text
The weight decay parameter in the optimizer turned negative
quiz.explain: Loss spikes were preceded by a collapse in the dynamic loss scalar and an uncontrolled rise in the L2-norm of the final layer activations.

quiz.q: How did base OPT-175B respond when researchers fed it direct declarative instructions?
options: It executed them with step-by-step reasoning
It crashed due to a sequence length overflow
It roleplayed a conversational dialogue starting with the command rather than carrying it out
It returned empty strings because it lacked a chat token
quiz.explain: As an unaligned base model, OPT-175B treated direct instructions as the opening line of a dialogue between two characters rather than a command to execute.

glossary.definition: Capabilities that do not appear in smaller models but surface abruptly once model size, training compute, or data reach a critical threshold.
The ability of a language model to complete novel tasks simply from natural language instructions and input demonstrations provided in the prompt, without updating its weights.
Fine-tuning a pre-trained model on diverse tasks formatted as explicit natural language instructions to enable zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback; a method that aligns model behavior with human intent by training a reward model on comparison data and optimizing the policy with reinforcement learning.
A prompting technique where a model generates intermediate reasoning steps before delivering the final answer to a complex problem.

quiz.q: According to the Chinchilla scaling law analyzed in the survey, how should compute budget be allocated when scaling up?
options: Model parameters should grow much faster than data tokens
Data token count and model parameter count should grow in roughly equal proportions
Token count should stay fixed while model depth quadruples
Compute budget should be spent exclusively on reinforcement learning
quiz.explain: Hoffmann et al. showed that under compute-optimal scaling, model parameter count and training token count should be scaled in approximately equal proportions.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an emergent ability from ordinary scaling behavior?
options: It appears smoothly and predictably at every single model size
It requires training without subword tokenization
It is absent in smaller models and rises sharply above random chance only after crossing a size threshold
It only occurs when fine-tuning on proprietary data
quiz.explain: Emergent abilities are defined by their sudden appearance: small models fail entirely, but once scale passes a specific threshold, task accuracy leaps dramatically.

quiz.q: Why is dataset deduplication so strictly emphasized before pre-training?
options: It converts all natural language into executable Python scripts
It prevents benchmark contamination and improves training efficiency
It eliminates the need for positional embeddings in Transformers
It guarantees that the model will never hallucinate
quiz.explain: Deduplication stops models from memorizing repeated web spam and prevents pre-training data from accidentally leaking test sets into the model weights.

glossary.definition: A lightweight 188-million parameter transformer that extracts language-aligned visual features using learned query tokens.
A compression mechanism where fixed query vectors compress high-dimensional image representations into a small set of informative tokens.
A pre-training objective that pulls representations of matching image-text pairs closer together while pushing unmatched pairs apart.
A generative pre-training task where a model produces the matching caption conditioned on visual query features.
A binary classification task that trains the model to decide whether a given image and caption truly belong together.

quiz.q: Why does BLIP-2 freeze both the vision encoder and the LLM during pre-training?
options: To save massive amounts of compute and prevent the models from forgetting their original capabilities
Because backpropagation cannot mathematically pass through two different architectures
To avoid needing any text captions during training
Because frozen models run significantly faster at inference time
quiz.explain: Freezing off-the-shelf vision models and LLMs saves huge training costs and protects the models from catastrophic forgetting.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the 32 learned queries in the Q-Former?
options: To act as an information bottleneck that distills text-relevant features from the frozen image encoder
To replace the text tokenizer inside the language model
To classify images into 32 predefined visual categories
To generate raw image pixels from text inputs
quiz.explain: The 32 queries interact with image features through cross-attention to extract only the visual information most useful for language.

quiz.q: Why did BLIP-2 struggle with few-shot in-context learning compared to models like Flamingo?
options: Its language model backbone was too small to understand prompts
Its pre-training data consisted only of single image-text pairs rather than interleaved web documents
Vision transformers cannot process more than one image at test time
The Q-Former is mathematically restricted to a single forward pass per conversation
quiz.explain: BLIP-2 trained exclusively on single image-caption pairs, so it never saw sequences containing multiple images and texts arranged together.

An open-source chatbot fine-tuned from LLaMA on user-shared conversations that serves as the frozen language decoder in MiniGPT-4.
A single linear matrix layer used to project visual representation vectors into the same dimensionality and embedding space as the LLM's text tokens.
Caption Hallucination Assessment with Image Relevance, a metric that evaluates hallucination by measuring the proportion of mentioned objects not present in the image.
Continuous vector representations fed directly into a language model's input sequence as if they were standard text token embeddings.

quiz.q: Why was a second-stage finetuning process necessary after pretraining on 5 million image-text pairs?
options: The vision encoder forgot how to recognize basic shapes
Noisy web captions caused the model to produce repetitive, fragmented, and unnatural text
The linear layer required retraining with a lower learning rate on GPU clusters
The model could not output tokens faster than one word per minute
quiz.explain: Pretraining on short, noisy web caption datasets led to language degradation like stuttering and fragmented sentences; 3,500 curated detailed pairs restored conversational fluency.

quiz.q: What did the ablation study reveal about removing the Q-Former from MiniGPT-4?
options: Performance completely collapsed on visual question answering benchmarks
The model achieved comparable scores, showing the Q-Former was not strictly required for advanced multimodal skills
Training time jumped from 10 hours to over 100 hours
The model lost the ability to generate HTML code from sketches
quiz.explain: The variant without Q-Former achieved 56.9 on AOK-VQA (vs 58.2) and 33.4 on GQA (vs 32.2), demonstrating that mapping ViT outputs directly through a linear layer retains most advanced multimodal skills.

glossary.definition: Making an AI system's behaviour match what its users and designers actually intend, such as being helpful, honest and harmless.
Training a pre-trained model further on examples of the desired behaviour, here prompts paired with ideal responses written by people.
A model trained to predict which of several responses humans would prefer, giving a score that stands in for human judgement.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: optimising a model to maximise a reward model trained on human preferences.
A term that discourages the fine-tuned model from drifting too far from its starting point, which helps prevent it from gaming the reward model.
A drop in performance on some standard tasks that can come with alignment training.
When a language model states made-up information as if it were true.

quiz.q: What are the three steps of the InstructGPT training recipe?
options: Supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, training a reward model on human rankings, then optimising with reinforcement learning
Collect images, label them, train a classifier

quiz.explain: Without it, the model could find strange outputs that score highly with the reward model but that humans would dislike.

Putting a handful of worked examples in the prompt so the model can imitate their format on a new question.
One worked example included in a prompt to show the model what to do.
An ability that is absent in smaller models and appears only once models pass a certain scale.
A standard set of test questions used to compare models fairly.
A follow-up technique that samples many different reasoning chains and takes the most common final answer.

options: Each example answer includes the intermediate reasoning steps, not just the final answer
The prompt is written in code

It only gave large gains for very large models, around 100 billion parameters and up

Knowledge stored outside the model, such as a collection of documents, that the model can search and read.

A task that a person could not reasonably do without looking up facts, such as answering open trivia questions.
A precomputed, searchable store of document embeddings that makes fast nearest-neighbour lookup possible.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of memory combined in RAG?

Two copies of the same model

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Fine-Tune a Giant by Training a Tiny Add-On
articles.subtitle: LoRA: freeze the huge model, learn two skinny matrices, and cut trainable parameters by up to ten thousand times

glossary.definition: Further training a pre-trained model on a specific task or dataset.
A grid of learned numbers inside a layer that transforms its input vector into an output vector.
Roughly, the number of independent directions a matrix can represent. A low-rank matrix can be written as the product of two thin matrices.
A small set of extra trainable parameters added to a frozen pre-trained model so it can learn a new task.
Parameters that are kept fixed during training and receive no updates.
How long a model takes to produce an output once it is deployed.

quiz.q: What does LoRA train during fine-tuning?
options: Only two small low-rank matrices per adapted weight matrix, while the original weights stay frozen
quiz.explain: The weight update is represented as B times A, two thin matrices, and only they are trained.

quiz.q: Why does LoRA add no extra delay when the model is deployed?
options: Because the learned update B times A can be added into the original weight matrix before deployment
Because it uses a faster GPU
It does add a large delay
quiz.explain: W plus BA is just another matrix of the same size, so the deployed model has exactly the original architecture.

quiz.q: Why is B initialised to zero?
options: So that at the start of training the update BA is zero and the model behaves exactly like the pre-trained model
Because random values are not allowed

It trains a secondary neural verifier to filter bad tokens.
It forces the model to write code rather than natural language.

CoT uses code interpreters for math, whereas ToT relies exclusively on token probabilities.

By querying an external reinforcement learning value model like AlphaGo.
By prompting the language model itself to deliberate, value (such as sure/maybe/impossible), or vote among states.
By measuring the length and vocabulary diversity of each generated thought.

Splitting a single model across several GPUs because it is too large to fit on one.
A form of model parallelism that splits the matrices inside each layer across GPUs, so every GPU computes part of every layer.

The GPU's small on-chip memory, close to the compute units: extremely fast but only a few hundred kilobytes per unit.
Designed around the cost of moving data between levels of memory, not just around the number of arithmetic operations.
Breaking a large computation into small blocks that fit in fast memory, and processing them one at a time.
Computing a softmax incrementally, block by block, by keeping a running maximum and running sum and rescaling as new blocks arrive.
A single program that runs on the GPU to perform one operation, such as a matrix multiply or a whole attention computation.
Recalculating intermediate values during the backward pass instead of storing them, trading extra arithmetic for less memory.

options: Reading and writing the large attention matrix to and from slow GPU main memory
quiz.explain: Attention spends most of its time moving data to and from HBM, not computing. FlashAttention reduces that traffic.

quiz.q: Does FlashAttention approximate attention?
options: Yes, it drops most of the attention weights
No, it computes exactly the same result as standard attention, just in a different order
Yes, it only attends to nearby tokens
quiz.explain: It is exact. The speedup comes from reorganising the computation, not from skipping any of it.

quiz.q: How can FlashAttention compute a softmax without seeing all the scores at once?
options: It keeps a running maximum and running sum, and rescales earlier partial results when a new block changes the maximum
It sorts all the scores first
quiz.explain: The online softmax trick lets each block be processed and combined correctly as it streams through fast memory.

How many requests or tokens a serving system completes per second.
Processing many users' requests together on the GPU so its parallel hardware is used efficiently.
Wasted memory caused by reserving space that is not used, or by gaps between allocations that are too small to reuse.
An operating system technique that maps a program's contiguous-looking addresses onto scattered physical pages of memory.
In PagedAttention, the map from each sequence's logical blocks of tokens to the physical memory blocks where their keys and values are stored.
Letting several users share the same memory until one of them needs to change it, and only then making a private copy.

quiz.q: What problem did existing serving systems have with the KV cache?

They reserved large contiguous chunks for the maximum possible length, wasting most of the memory through fragmentation
They deleted it after every token

quiz.q: How does PagedAttention store each sequence's KV cache?
options: In one big contiguous block sized for the maximum length
In small fixed-size blocks that can sit anywhere in memory, tracked by a block table, like pages in virtual memory
quiz.explain: Non-contiguous blocks are allocated on demand, so almost no memory is wasted and blocks can be shared between sequences.

glossary.definition: The integer value in the quantized domain that corresponds exactly to real-world value 0.0, ensuring zero-padding operations introduce no numerical bias.
A positive floating-point factor that represents the step size between adjacent quantized integer values.
An operation during model training that clamps and rounds floating-point values to discrete levels, simulating quantization noise during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients.
Algebraically absorbing the scaling and shift parameters of batch normalization directly into preceding convolutional weights and biases prior to quantization.
General Matrix Multiply, the primary computational kernel underpinning fully connected and convolutional operations in neural networks.

quiz.q: Why are bias vectors quantized as 32-bit integers rather than 8-bit integers?
options: Biases account for most model parameters, so precision is critical.
Bias quantization error acts as a nonzero-mean offset across many outputs, degrading accuracy.
8-bit hardware does not support addition operations.
Hardware accumulators cannot add different bit widths together.
quiz.explain: Each bias entry is added to many output activations; any quantization error introduces a systematic nonzero-mean shift, degrading end-to-end model accuracy.

quiz.q: How is floating-point scaling applied during integer-only inference when converting accumulators back to 8 bits?
options: Via floating-point lookup tables stored in ROM.
By normalizing the scale multiplier into M = 2^(-n) * M0 and executing fixed-point integer multiplication with a bit-shift.
By ignoring the scale factors and rounding integers directly.
quiz.explain: The multiplier M is factored into an integer fixed-point multiplier M0 (in [0.5, 1)) and a power-of-two shift 2^(-n), allowing pure integer hardware to apply the scale.

quiz.q: Why is batch normalization 'folded' into weights before quantization?
options: Batch normalization layers cannot be computed on mobile CPUs.
To accurately simulate during training the weights that will actually appear in inference.
Folding eliminates all activation functions in the network.
To increase the bit-depth of weights from 8 bits to 16 bits.
quiz.explain: Inference engines fold batch normalization parameters directly into convolutional weights for speed; simulating this folding during training ensures the quantized weights match inference.

Pick a data structure at random

The smallest version of the problem, answered directly without another recursive call. It stops the recursion.
The step that reduces the problem to one or more smaller versions and combines their answers.
The memory where the computer keeps each unfinished function call, with its own variables, until it returns.
A drawing of every call a recursive function makes, used to count total work.
A crash that happens when recursion goes so deep that the call stack runs out of memory.

quiz.q: What happens if a recursive function has no reachable base case?

quiz.explain: Without a base case the calls never stop, each one using stack memory, until a stack overflow.

quiz.q: How many calls does the naive recursive Fibonacci make for fib(5)?

options: Assuming the recursive call correctly solves the smaller problem, and only checking that you use its answer correctly
quiz.explain: You reason about one level at a time: if the smaller call is right, is this level right? Together with a correct base case, that proves the whole function.

An operator that works on each bit position separately: AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~).
Moving all bits left or right. Shifting left by k multiplies by 2 to the power k; shifting right divides, rounding down for non-negative numbers.
A number whose 1 bits mark the positions you care about, used to test, set or clear those bits.
The standard way computers store negative integers, where -x is ~x + 1.
The rightmost bit, worth 1. It decides whether a number is odd or even.

quiz.q: What is 13 & 6? (13 is 1101, 6 is 0110 in binary)
quiz.explain: AND keeps a 1 only where both numbers have a 1. 1101 & 0110 = 0100, which is 4.

quiz.explain: Shift x right by k so bit k lands in the last position, then AND with 1 to read just that bit.

quiz.q: Why write 1LL << 40 instead of 1 << 40?
options: 1 is an int, usually 32 bits, so shifting it by 40 is undefined; 1LL is a 64-bit long long
quiz.explain: Shifting a 32-bit int by 32 or more is undefined behaviour. Making the 1 a long long gives 64 bits of room.

glossary.definition: The total of all elements from the start of an array up to a given position.
A question about a contiguous slice of an array, such as the sum of elements from index l to index r.
Doing work once, up front, so that many later questions become cheap to answer.
An array that stores how much each element changes compared with the one before it. Its prefix sums rebuild the original array.
An extra value placed at the edge of a data structure, like a leading zero, so edge cases disappear from the code.

quiz.q: With P[i] defined as the sum of the first i elements (so P[0] = 0), what is the sum of a[l..r] (0-indexed, inclusive)?
quiz.explain: P[r + 1] covers a[0..r] and P[l] covers a[0..l-1]. Subtracting removes everything before l.

quiz.q: Why does the leading zero in the prefix array help?
options: It removes the special case for ranges that start at index 0
quiz.explain: Without it, a range starting at 0 would need P[-1]. The extra 0 at the front acts as a sentinel, so one formula works for every range.

quiz.q: You must add 5 to every element in 100,000 different ranges, then print the final array once. What is the best tool?
options: Update each range element by element
Rebuild the prefix sum after every update
A difference array, then one prefix-sum pass at the end
quiz.explain: A difference array records each range update in O(1) with two edits. One prefix-sum pass at the end turns it back into the final array.

glossary.definition: Here, simply an index into the array that marks a position you are looking at.
Two indices that start at the two ends of an array and move toward each other.
Two indices that both move left to right, one leading and one following, also called fast and slow pointers.
A fact that stays true at every step of a loop, which is what lets you prove the algorithm is correct.
Always moving in one direction, never backwards. Both pointers only ever move forward, which bounds the total work.

quiz.q: In a sorted array, the current pair sums to more than the target. Which pointer moves?
quiz.explain: The right value is the largest in play. Pairing it with anything at or after left is still too big, so it can be discarded by moving right leftwards.

quiz.q: Why is the two-pointer scan O(n) and not O(n squared)?
options: Each step moves one pointer inward and neither ever moves back, so there are at most n steps
It stops at the first pair
It only works on small arrays
quiz.explain: The gap between the pointers shrinks by one every step, so the loop runs at most n times.

quiz.q: In 3Sum, why do we sort first?
options: So that for each fixed first number, the remaining pair can be found with two pointers and duplicates can be skipped easily
Because the output must be sorted
quiz.explain: Sorting enables the inward squeeze for the remaining two numbers and puts equal values next to each other, so duplicates are easy to skip.

articles.title: The Caterpillar That Reads Arrays in One Pass

glossary.definition: A contiguous stretch of an array or string, described by a left and a right index.
A window that always contains exactly k elements and slides one step at a time.
A window whose right edge grows and whose left edge shrinks according to a validity rule.
The summary you keep about the current window, such as its sum or a count of each character, updated as elements enter and leave.
Averaged over the whole run. Each element enters and leaves the window once, so the total work is linear even if one step does a lot.

quiz.q: In a variable-size window, why must the shrinking step be a while loop and not an if?
options: Adding one element can make the window invalid by more than one step, so you may need to remove several elements
quiz.explain: One new element can break the rule badly, for example a long run of repeats. You keep removing from the left until the window is valid again.

quiz.q: Why can a plain sliding window fail for 'shortest subarray with sum at least k' when negative numbers exist?
options: Shrinking the window may increase its sum, so 'shrink while too big' no longer moves toward the answer
Hash maps do not support negatives
quiz.explain: The window logic assumes growing makes the sum bigger and shrinking makes it smaller. Negatives break that, so prefix sums with a monotonic deque are used instead.

options: O(n squared) because of the nested while loop
O(n), because each element enters once and leaves at most once
quiz.explain: The inner while loop looks nested, but the left pointer only moves forward, so across the whole run it moves at most n times.

glossary.definition: A structure that stores key-value pairs and finds a key in constant time on average by turning it into a bucket number.
The value you still need to reach a target, such as target minus the current number.
A hash map from each item to how many times it has appeared.
A standard form of an item, such as its sorted letters, chosen so that items that belong together get the same key.
When two different keys land in the same bucket of a hash table, which slows lookups if it happens a lot.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time of a single unordered_map lookup?
quiz.explain: It is O(1) on average, but if many keys land in the same bucket, a lookup may scan all of them.

glossary.definition: A contiguous, non-empty slice of an array, like elements 3 to 7. Order is kept and nothing is skipped.
The largest sum of any subarray that ends exactly at the current index. Kadane's algorithm keeps only this one number.
The best answer seen so far over all positions, updated after each step.
Solving a problem by building answers to small subproblems and reusing them, instead of recomputing.

options: Whether to extend the best subarray ending at i-1 or start fresh at i
quiz.explain: The best subarray ending at i either continues the best one ending at i-1, or starts at i alone. Take whichever sum is larger.

quiz.explain: Subarrays must be non-empty, so the best is the single element -1. Initialising the answer to 0 is a classic bug.

options: A very negative product can become the largest after multiplying by a negative number

glossary.definition: An array of 26 counters, one per lowercase letter, used instead of a hash map when the alphabet is small and fixed.
A word formed by rearranging all the letters of another, like 'listen' and 'silent'.
A string that reads the same forwards and backwards, like 'racecar' or 'abba'.
Finding palindromes by starting from each possible middle and growing outwards while both ends match.
A string that cannot be changed in place, so every 'change' creates a new copy. In C++ std::string is mutable, but s = s + c still builds a new string.

quiz.q: How do you check if two lowercase strings are anagrams in O(n)?
options: Sort both and compare in O(n)
Count letters with one array of 26: add for the first string, subtract for the second, and check all zero
quiz.explain: Anagrams have identical letter counts. One frequency array, incremented for one string and decremented for the other, ends at all zeros exactly when they match.

options: 2n − 1, because even-length palindromes have a centre between two characters
quiz.explain: Each character is an odd-length centre, and each gap between neighbours is an even-length centre: n + (n − 1) centres.

quiz.q: Why is s = s + c inside a loop over n characters slow?
options: Each step copies the whole string built so far, so the total work is O(n squared)
quiz.explain: s + c creates a new string of the current length each time. Use s += c or push_back, which append in amortised O(1).

Two intervals overlap when one starts before the other ends.
Replacing overlapping intervals with one interval that covers all of them.
A technique that processes events in sorted order, as if a line moved across the timeline, keeping a running state.
A point where something changes, such as an interval starting (+1) or ending (-1).

glossary.definition: The product of all elements before a given position, like a running total but multiplying.
The product of all elements after a given position.
Scanning an array once from the left and once from the right, combining what each pass learned.
The array you must return. Problems often say it does not count as extra space, which allows reusing it as a workspace.

quiz.q: For index i, the answer equals...
options: The total product divided by nums[i]
The product of everything left of i times the product of everything right of i
quiz.explain: Everything except nums[i] is exactly the left part and the right part, so multiply their products.

quiz.q: Why is dividing the total product by nums[i] a bad idea?
options: It fails when nums[i] is 0, and the problem forbids division anyway
quiz.explain: A zero in the array makes the total 0 and division by zero undefined. The prefix-suffix method needs no division at all.

quiz.q: How does the O(1) extra space version avoid a separate suffix array?
options: It recomputes suffixes for each i
It stores prefix products in the output array, then sweeps from the right with a single running suffix variable
It cannot; O(n) space is required
quiz.explain: The output array holds left products after the first pass; one variable carries the right product during the second pass.

glossary.definition: A contiguous, non-empty slice of an array.
The total of all elements from the start of the array up to a position.
A hash map from a value to how many times it has been seen so far.
Here, the earlier prefix sum you need, P minus k, so that the subarray between them sums to k.

quiz.q: If P[j] is the prefix sum through j and P[i] is the prefix sum before i, what is the sum of elements i through j?
quiz.explain: The difference of two running totals is the total of the stretch between them.

quiz.q: Why must the map start with {0: 1}?
options: It represents the empty prefix before the array, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted
quiz.explain: A subarray from index 0 to j sums to k when P[j] − 0 = k. The empty prefix with sum 0 must already be in the map for that to be found.

One past the last candidate, so the answer lies in [lo, hi)

options: It avoids integer overflow when lo and hi are large

An extra node placed before the head so that edits at the front work exactly like edits in the middle.

glossary.definition: The limits printed under the input format, such as 1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁵, which reveal the required complexity.

The small example inputs and outputs in the statement. They show the format but rarely the hard cases.
The narrative wrapper around a problem, like a tale about cows or shops, which usually hides a standard task.

quiz.explain: Constraints tell you which complexities are allowed and the output format tells you exactly what to produce. The story can be skimmed afterwards.

quiz.explain: Samples are chosen to explain the format, not to catch bugs. Edge cases you check yourself catch the Wrong Answers that samples miss.

A slow but obviously correct solution, used here only as a referee on tiny inputs.

An input on which the fast and brute-force solutions disagree, which pinpoints the bug.

options: The brute force must be fast enough, and a tiny counterexample is easy to debug by hand
quiz.explain: Most bugs show up on small inputs. Tiny tests keep the brute force fast and give you a failing case you can trace on paper.

quiz.explain: With the seed, you can reproduce the same random input any time, which turns a flaky failure into a fixed test case.

Stress tests always find every bug
You need more seeds of the same tiny size only

The next one or two problems just beyond what you solved
Only the ones you already solved

You must print the lexicographically smallest
Output order does not matter at all

A quantity that only ever moves in one direction, such as a count that can only decrease, which proves a process must end.
Whether a number is even or odd. Many moves change numbers but keep their parity.
Something that must be true for an answer to exist. An invariant usually gives one.
Something that, when true, guarantees an answer exists. Proving it usually needs a construction.

options: Every move removes exactly 3 coins in total
It does not need to be

options: A proof or construction showing every remaining input really is solvable
A brute force for all n
quiz.explain: An invariant gives a necessary condition. You still need to show it is sufficient, usually by constructing an answer, or by checking it against a brute force.

A fixed amount of time you allow yourself for a task before you stop and reassess.

options: Each wrong submission can cost penalty time or points, and a quick edge-case test is cheaper

What is left after dividing: 17 mod 5 is 2, because 17 = 3 × 5 + 2.
Two numbers are congruent modulo m when they have the same remainder after dividing by m.
When a result is too large for its type and wraps around to a wrong value.
A modulus that is a prime number, such as 10^9 + 7 or 998244353, which makes division possible through modular inverses.

quiz.q: Why is it safe to take the remainder after every addition and multiplication?
options: It is not safe; only take it at the end
Because (a + b) mod m and (a × b) mod m only depend on a mod m and b mod m
Because the judge rounds the answer
quiz.explain: Adding or multiplying the remainders gives the same final remainder as using the full numbers, so you can reduce at every step and keep numbers small.

quiz.explain: C++ keeps the sign of the left operand, so the result is -1. To get a value in [0, m), add m and take mod again: ((x % m) + m) % m.

An algorithm that finds all primes up to n by crossing out the multiples of each prime.

options: Every smaller multiple k × p with k < p has a smaller prime factor and was already crossed out
quiz.explain: A multiple k × p with k < p has a prime factor of k, which is smaller than p, so an earlier prime already crossed it out.
